title: Middle Eastern, South Asian & African Languages
summary: Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Turkish, Hindi, Bengali, Swahili, Yoruba and Amharic. Root-and-pattern morphology (Arabic, Hebrew) and agglutination (Turkish, Swahili) are the thresholds: words become formulas you can build, not lists you memorise.
sources: Ryding: A Reference Grammar of Modern Standard Arabic
Göksel & Kerslake: Turkish: A Comprehensive Grammar
Daniels & Bright: The World's Writing Systems

nodes.label: Arabic: Script & Sounds
nodes.summary: A cursive abjad written right to left; letters change shape by position.
nodes.outcome: Read Arabic letters in their joined forms.
nodes.check: In which direction is Arabic written?

nodes.label: Arabic: The Root System
nodes.summary: Most words are a three-consonant root poured into a vowel pattern. Once seen, vocabulary becomes a system you can generate.
nodes.outcome: Derive related words from one root.
nodes.check: Arabic words built on the root k-t-b (كتب) share what meaning?
nodes.answer: Writing (kitāb book, kātib writer, maktab office or desk).

nodes.label: Arabic: Basics
nodes.summary: Greetings and courtesy in Modern Standard Arabic.
nodes.check: How do you say 'thank you' in Arabic?

nodes.label: "All Arabic speakers speak the same Arabic"
nodes.summary: Spoken dialects differ widely; Modern Standard Arabic is shared for writing and formal speech.
nodes.check: Why might a Moroccan and an Iraqi struggle with each other's everyday Arabic?
nodes.answer: Spoken dialects differ greatly; Modern Standard Arabic is shared mainly for writing and formal speech (diglossia).

nodes.label: Hebrew: A Revived Language
nodes.summary: A Semitic root system and abjad, revived for everyday speech in modern times.
nodes.outcome: Read Hebrew letters and recognise shared Semitic roots.
nodes.check: In roughly which period was Hebrew revived as an everyday spoken language?

nodes.label: Persian (Farsi)
nodes.summary: Written in an Arabic-based script but Indo-European, with simple verbs and no grammatical gender.
nodes.outcome: Explain why Persian looks like Arabic but is related to English.
nodes.check: Which language family does Persian belong to?
nodes.answer: Indo-European (Iranian branch), not Semitic like Arabic.

nodes.label: Turkish: Agglutination & Vowel Harmony
nodes.summary: Suffixes stack in a fixed order, with vowels that harmonise with the stem.
nodes.outcome: Build and parse Turkish words suffix by suffix.
nodes.check: Turkish stacks suffixes: 'ev' (house) becomes 'evlerim'. What does 'evlerim' mean?

nodes.label: Hindi: Devanagari
nodes.summary: An abugida: consonants carry an inherent vowel, changed with vowel signs, under a headline.
nodes.check: What is the horizontal line along the top of Devanagari letters called?

nodes.label: Hindi: Basics
nodes.summary: SOV order, postpositions and respectful forms of address.
nodes.outcome: Greet respectfully and form simple Hindi sentences.
nodes.check: How do you greet someone respectfully in Hindi?

nodes.label: "Hindi and Urdu are completely different languages"
nodes.summary: In everyday speech they are largely one language (Hindustani), differing mainly in script and formal vocabulary.
nodes.outcome: Explain how Hindi and Urdu differ and overlap.
nodes.check: Why can Hindi and Urdu speakers usually understand each other in conversation?
nodes.answer: Colloquially they are largely the same language (Hindustani); they differ mainly in script and formal vocabulary.

nodes.label: Bengali
nodes.summary: One of the world's most spoken languages, with its own abugida.
nodes.outcome: Locate Bengali-speaking regions and read its script basics.
nodes.check: In which two countries is Bengali official, nationally or in a state?
nodes.answer: Bangladesh (national) and India (in West Bengal and Tripura).

nodes.label: Swahili: Noun Classes
nodes.summary: Nouns fall into classes marked by prefixes that agreement copies across the sentence.
nodes.outcome: Use Swahili noun-class prefixes and greet.
nodes.check: How do you say 'thank you' in Swahili?

nodes.label: Yoruba: A Tonal African Language
nodes.summary: Three level tones marked with accents in writing.
nodes.check: How many basic tones does Yoruba have?

nodes.label: Amharic: The Ge'ez Script
nodes.summary: A Semitic language written in an abugida of consonant–vowel characters.
nodes.outcome: Explain how the Ge'ez script encodes vowels.
nodes.check: What kind of writing system is the Ge'ez script used for Amharic?
nodes.answer: An abugida: each character is a consonant with a built-in vowel marking.
